<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This “aws-devops-zero-to-hero” repo is an open-source educational toolkit for learning AWS-centric DevOps practices over 30 days. It bundles per-day sample applications, Infrastructure-as-Code scripts, CI/CD definitions, monitoring demos, and a catalog of AWS interview questions.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level directories:  
     • day-* folders (day-1 through day-30): each contains code samples (Python apps, Dockerfiles, Terraform, CloudFormation, Lambda functions, shell scripts) illustrating a particular AWS service or DevOps workflow.  
     • interview-questions: markdown files covering AWS service theory and Q&A.  
     • scripts: generic helper scripts (start_container.sh, stop_container.sh).  
   - CI/CD and deployment manifests appear under day-14 (buildspec.yml, appspec.yml), day-21 (Dockerfile, requirements.txt), day-24 (Terraform .tf files), day-25 (Lambda function and permissions).  
   - No single “running system” emerges; instead, it’s a compendium of small demos that—when combined—form a canonical AWS DevOps pipeline and environment.  

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - The README outlines a 30-day curriculum covering:  
     IAM, EC2, VPC, S3, CLI, CloudFormation, CodeCommit/Build/Pipeline/Deploy, CloudWatch/Events, Lambda, CloudFront, ECR, ECS, EKS, Secrets Manager, Terraform, CloudTrail/Config, ELB, RDS, best practices, migration.  
   - It describes real-time projects for each day—each project exercises a subset of AWS services.  

4. Main components for your system-design diagram  
   a. Code Repository (Git/CodeCommit)  
   b. CI/CD Orchestration (CodePipeline)  
   c. Build & Test (CodeBuild, Docker build)  
   d. Artifact Registry (ECR for containers, S3 for static)  
   e. Deployment Engines  
      • Compute: EC2 (Day 3), ECS (Day 21), EKS (Day 22), Lambda (Day 17)  
      • Networking: VPC with subnets, IGW, NAT (Days 4 & 7)  
      • Storage: S3 (Day 9), EBS (Day 18 snapshots), RDS (Day 30)  
   f. Infrastructure as Code  
      • CloudFormation templates (Day 11)  
      • Terraform modules (Day 24)  
   g. Monitoring & Logging  
      • CloudWatch Metrics & Logs (Day 16)  
      • CloudWatch Events / EventBridge (Day 18)  
      • CloudTrail & Config (Day 25)  
   h. Security & Access  
      • IAM roles/policies (Day 2, Day 7)  
      • Secrets Manager (Day 23)  

5. Relationships and interactions  
   - Developer pushes code → Git/CodeCommit  
   - CodePipeline triggers → CodeBuild (runs buildspec.yml) → produces Docker images or zip artifacts  
   - Artifacts pushed to ECR or S3  
   - Deployment stage in CodePipeline uses CodeDeploy (appspec.yml) to update EC2/ECS/EKS/Lambda  
   - Deployed workloads run inside a secured VPC (public/private subnets, SGs, NACLs)  
   - Services log metrics to CloudWatch and send events to EventBridge  
   - CloudTrail records API calls; Config enforces compliance  
   - Secrets Manager supplies credentials at runtime  

6. Architectural patterns and design principles  
   - Modular demos align to AWS service boundaries (compute vs. storage vs. networking vs. CI/CD).  
   - CI/CD pipeline modeling continuous delivery with immutable artifacts (Docker images, Lambda packages).  
   - IaC ensures idempotent environment provisioning (CloudFormation, Terraform).  
   - Event-driven serverless workflows demonstrate decoupling (CloudWatch Events → Lambda).  
   - Multi-AZ high availability patterns (ELB, auto-scaling, private subnets).  

7. Diagramming guidelines  
   - Use distinct shapes/colors for:  
     • Developer tools & repo (e.g., rectangular “dev box” icon)  
     • CI/CD components (CodePipeline, CodeBuild — use AWS official icons)  
     • Compute resources (EC2, ECS tasks, EKS pods, Lambda)  
     • Storage & registry (S3 buckets, ECR repos, RDS instances, EBS volumes)  
     • Networking (VPC box, public/private subnets, IGW, NAT Gateway)  
     • Security (IAM roles, Secrets Manager vault)  
     • Monitoring (CloudWatch, CloudTrail, Config, EventBridge)  
   - Label every component clearly.  
   - Draw directional arrows to indicate:  
     • Git → CodePipeline  
     • CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR/S3  
     • CodePipeline → CodeDeploy → Compute services  
     • Compute services → CloudWatch & CloudTrail  
     • EventBridge → Lambda  
     • Secrets Manager → Compute services  
   - Group related services within dashed or colored containers (e.g., “CI/CD,” “Compute,” “Observability,” “Security”).  
   - Align services to AWS architectural zones: left (developer & CI/CD), center (compute & networking), right (monitoring & security).  

8. Tailoring for this educational repo  
   - Emphasize how each “day-N” demo plugs into the overall pipeline: e.g., Day-14’s Dockerized Python app runs through the same build & deploy flow as the Day-21 ECS service.  
   - Highlight extensibility by showing placeholders for additional day modules (e.g., “Day-17: Lambda Demo” box).  
   - Show IaC overlay layers (CloudFormation/Terraform) that can tear down and rebuild all components.  

By following these guidelines, you’ll produce a comprehensive, accurate system-design diagram that maps the aws-devops-zero-to-hero repo’s educational modules onto a real-world AWS DevOps architecture—making it easy for learners (and stakeholders) to see how individual demos coalesce into a full, production-grade pipeline and environment.  
</explanation>
